headline: United has made up 77% of a fuel cost shock in the long run (90% range 61% to 279%), half of it within 1.0 quarters (0.4 to 13.5).
plain_summary: United has made up 77% of a fuel cost shock in the long run (90% range 61% to 279%), half of it within 1.0 quarters (0.4 to 13.5).

The curve the simulator reads (through latest, 30 quarters to 2026Q2, 90% ranges): L = 77% (61% to 279%), rho = 0.50 (0.19 to 0.95), half-life 1.0 quarters (0.4 to 13.5), one-year share 75% (49% to 91%).
By quarter after the shock its middle estimate is 18% (12% to 50%), 33% (23% to 66%), 45% (33% to 75%), 54% (43% to 79%), 62% (51% to 83%), with P10 to P90 in brackets.
On the fit split alone (20 quarters): L = 97% (33% to 222%), rho = 0.78 (0.00 to 0.92), half-life 2.8 quarters (0.0 to 8.3), one-year share 69% (33% to 107%).

Rival comparison on the 10 locked test quarters, four quarters ahead, average miss in cents per ASM: 0.56 for the smooth curve fitted on the fit split, 1.14 for no response, 0.59 for full immediate recovery, 0.56 for management's path and 0.73 for the pre-specified five-lag curve.
The speed of the published curve rests on one quarter.
Fitted through 2026Q1 the half-life is 2.8 quarters (rho 0.78, L 91%); adding 2026Q2 alone makes it 1.0 (rho 0.50, L 77%).
Bootstrap resamples that leave that quarter out give slow curves, so the middle of the draws (18% in the shock quarter, 62% after a year) is slower than the least-squares curve (39% and 75%).
The simulator samples the draws.
This two-parameter form was chosen AFTER the locked test years had been seen, because the pre-specified five-lag curve was not monotone and lost the test.
Its test-split score is therefore descriptive, not a clean test.
The clean test of it is the dated forward forecast for the next quarter.
One quarter after a fuel cost shock the fitted share is 58% (90% range 22% to 74%, 30 quarters): more than nothing, less than the 80% to 90% management stated for 2026Q3.
The pre-specified result stands and follows.

After a fuel cost shock, United's unit revenue has made up 3% of the cost in the same quarter and 75% a year later (90% ranges -27% to 33% and 51% to 99%, 20 quarters): a response is clear, and the range stops short of the full cost within a year.

One quarter after a fuel cost shock the fitted share is 80% (90% range 47% to 112%, 20 quarters): that is consistent with the 80% to 90% management stated for 2026Q3, and no recovery is outside the range.
Fitted on 20 quarters (2015Q1 to 2019Q4), the share made up is 4% in the quarter of the shock (P10 -19%, P90 27%), 79% one quarter later (P10 54%, P90 102%) and 75% after a year (P10 57%, P90 94%).

Locked test, four quarters ahead (n = 10 quarters): mean absolute error in cents per ASM is 1.14 for no response, 0.59 for full immediate recovery, 0.56 for management's path, 0.73 for the pre-specified five-lag curve; lowest is management's path.
The pre-specified curve minus management's path: +0.17, 90% range -0.20 to +0.41, which includes zero.

Locked test, one quarter ahead (n = 9 quarters): mean absolute error in cents per ASM is 0.79 for no response, 0.76 for full immediate recovery, 0.69 for management's path, 0.84 for the pre-specified five-lag curve; lowest is management's path.
The pre-specified curve minus management's path: +0.15, 90% range -0.08 to +0.44, which includes zero.
The select split (2020-2023) has 0 quarters free of pandemic-period levels, so its scores are reported but decide nothing.

For 2026Q2 the raw ratio of United's revenue change to its fuel expense change is 1.04; the fitted model assigns 3% of the fuel cost change per ASM to recovery; United said it recovered about 50%, which implies an undisclosed baseline revenue growth of 8.3%.
This compares definitions; it does not validate either.
Not stable across periods.

Re-estimated on all 30 quarters through 2026Q2 with no pandemic level behind them (test years included; not used for the curve), the same-quarter share is 53% (12% to 95%) against 3% on the fit split, and the one-year share 83% (53% to 113%) against 75%.
Second look, Delta (in sample on 12 quarters, 11 of them in the test years, 7 coefficients): 68% in the same quarter (27% to 109%) and 198% a year later (110% to 286%).

United's rules on Delta's quarters, four quarters ahead, fuel term only (n = 11): 0.86 for no response, 0.52 for full immediate recovery, 0.55 for management's path, 0.87 for the pre-specified five-lag curve; lowest is full immediate recovery.

Industry fares: a 10% rise in jet fuel goes with a +0.44% change in real airfares over 12 months (90% range -0.67% to +1.55%, 84 months): the range includes zero, so this history cannot tell a fare response from none.
Fuel increases and decreases: the 12-month fare elasticities are -0.010 and 0.003; the test that they are equal gives p = 0.95.
recovery_definition: The published curve is recovery(k) = L x (1 - rho^(k+1)): L is the share of a lasting fuel cost change that unit revenue makes up in the long run, rho how much of the remaining gap stays open each quarter. It is fitted to the same quantities as before. Recovery share k quarters after a fuel cost shock = the change in United's total revenue per available seat mile (cents) in that quarter per one-cent lasting change in fuel cost per available seat mile, at given capacity growth. In the pre-specified version (curve_unrestricted) it is the running sum through lag k of the coefficients from regressing the year-over-year change in TRASM on the year-over-year changes in fuel cost per ASM (average price per gallon times gallons, over ASM) at lags 0 to 4, with year-over-year capacity growth as a control. It is a share in that quarter, not a running total of dollars, and after quarter 4 it is held. A share of 1 means unit revenue is up by as much as unit fuel cost. How this relates to United's measure: United says it 'recovered' a share of the year-over-year increase in fuel expense but discloses no formula. The raw ratio of its revenue change to its fuel expense change does not reproduce its figure, so its measure must be (revenue change minus a baseline revenue change that would have happened without the fuel move) divided by the fuel expense change, with a baseline it does not disclose. Ours has the same form with a stated baseline: the fitted constant plus the fitted effect of capacity growth, estimated on 2013-2019. The two baselines need not agree, so our share and United's are not the same number.

primary_spec.description: Two-parameter partial-adjustment recovery curve on the same data and definition as the five-lag regression, with the capacity control; the curve the simulator and the forward test read.
primary_spec.equation: d4(TRASM)[t] = a + L * sum_{j=0..4} (1 - rho) rho^j * d4(fuel cost per ASM)[t-j] + c * capacity growth[t] + e[t]; recovery share at k = L * (1 - rho^(k+1))
primary_spec.sample: 2015Q1 to 2026Q2, no quarter with a 2020Q1-2021Q4 level behind it
primary_spec.post_hoc_note: This two-parameter form was chosen AFTER the locked test years had been seen, because the pre-specified five-lag curve was not monotone and lost the test. Its test-split score is therefore descriptive, not a clean test. The clean test of it is the dated forward forecast for the next quarter.
primary_spec.why_through_latest: A forward-looking simulation may use everything known today. Replays of past quarters must use smooth.expanding, which never sees its own future.

prespecified.description: Year-over-year change in TRASM (cents) on year-over-year change in fuel cost per ASM (cents, price per gallon times gallons over ASM) at lags 0 to 4, controlling for year-over-year capacity growth; fit split only. Primary.
prespecified.equation: d4(TRASM)[t] = a + sum_{j=0..4} b[j] * d4(fuel cost per ASM)[t-j] + c * capacity growth[t] + e[t]; recovery share at k = b[0] + ... + b[k]
prespecified.units: cents per available seat mile; capacity growth in percent year over year
prespecified.standard_errors: Standard errors come from a cautious covariance: the classical one plus the positive part of (Newey-West minus classical), which is at least as large as both for every coefficient and every sum of coefficients. Newey-West errors are biased downward in short samples and can fall below the classical ones; this never reports the smaller. Intervals use Student t with the residual degrees of freedom. Newey-West lag for the quarterly regressions: 4 (year-over-year changes overlap by three quarters).
prespecified.pandemic_handling: Primary: estimated on the fit split only, which ends in 2019Q4, so no pandemic quarter enters as an observation or behind a change. Variants: 2013-2023 excluding pandemic-touched quarters, and 2013-2023 with quarter indicators.
prespecified.why_primary: It is the specification named in the project brief and was fixed before any select or test number was computed. Fit-only estimation keeps both later splits out of the coefficients. The capacity control matches the simulator, which moves capacity separately. No variant was promoted on select-split scores, because every select quarter is pandemic-touched.
prespecified.industry: Monthly log change in real airfares (CUSR0000SETG01 over CUSR0000SA0) on log changes in monthly average jet fuel, lags 0 to 12, 2013-2019. Primary industry specification.

curve_draws_method.method: Partial adjustment: recovery(k) = L x (1 - rho^(k+1)) for k = 0..4 quarters after the shock. L is the share recovered in the long run and rho the part of the remaining gap left open each quarter; the half-life, ln(0.5)/ln(rho), counts quarters from the start of the shock quarter until half of L is in. Same data and definition as the five-lag regression: year-over-year change in TRASM on a constant, year-over-year capacity growth and L times the weighted sum of the year-over-year fuel cost changes at lags 0 to 4 with weights (1 - rho) rho^j. Least squares: rho on a grid from 0 to 0.95 in steps of 0.01, L in closed form given rho. Uncertainty: a moving-block bootstrap over quarters (blocks of four consecutive estimation rows, each row carrying its own lags), L and rho re-estimated on every resample; ranges are percentiles of the resamples and the draws are the resampled curves. Where the estimation rows are not contiguous (2019Q4 is followed by 2024Q1) a block can straddle the gap. The curve stops at quarter 4, where the share is L x (1 - rho^5).
curve_draws_method.why: A bootstrap rather than a covariance: the curve is non-linear in rho, and resampling quarters carries the trade-off between L and rho into the draws. Every draw is monotone by construction.

industry_monthly_definition: coef is the cumulative elasticity of real airfares to jet fuel through that lag (the sum of the lag coefficients 0..lag), lo and hi its 90% interval; lag_coef is the single lag's coefficient. Standard errors come from a cautious covariance: the classical one plus the positive part of (Newey-West minus classical), which is at least as large as both for every coefficient and every sum of coefficients. Newey-West errors are biased downward in short samples and can fall below the classical ones; this never reports the smaller. Intervals use Student t with the residual degrees of freedom.

recovery_share_conversion.formula: recovery share through lag k = cumulative fare elasticity through lag k / (fuel expense / total revenue): full recovery of a fuel cost change needs revenue to change by that share times the percentage change in fuel
recovery_share_conversion.caveat: The share is United's, used for an industry price index; the interval carries the elasticity's uncertainty only. The elasticity is of real fares to the nominal fuel price.

limits: Co-movement, not a causal pass-through: fuel prices and travel demand rise and fall together with the economy, so part of any measured response is demand, not airlines passing on cost. Nothing here identifies the causal share.

The industry measure is the consumer price index for airline fares: fares paid by consumers, not airline revenue per seat mile. It leaves out most ancillary revenue, and the seasonally adjusted series is the current vintage, revised annually, not the figures first published.
The industry result is an elasticity of fares to fuel, not a recovery share. Converting it needs fuel cost as a share of revenue, and the share used is United's, not the industry's.
October 2025 has no CPI print in the source (2025-10); the two monthly changes that touch a missing month are left out, not interpolated.

The pandemic breaks every airline series. Monthly: March 2020 to December 2021; quarterly: 2020Q1 to 2021Q4 (the brief says roughly 2020Q2; the collapse began in March 2020, inside 2020Q1). The primary estimates use the fit split, which ends in 2019. With year-over-year changes and four lags, every quarter from 2020Q1 to 2023Q4 has a pandemic-quarter level somewhere behind it, so the select split cannot discriminate between specifications for the quarterly curve.

Timing inside a quarter is not measured. The curve is estimated on year-over-year changes in quarterly averages, so quarter 0 is the response to a change in the quarter's average fuel cost, however that change was spread over the quarter in the fitting years. It does not say what happens when fuel jumps late in a quarter, after most of that quarter's seats are sold: the jump moves the quarter's average only a little, the curve applies its quarter-0 share to that small change, and the rest of the jump arrives as next quarter's shock. It cannot separate fuel that has been high for a while from fuel that moved after guidance was set, and the simulator's monthly reading of the curve (one step per quarter) is not a within-quarter path. Delta's September 2026 quarter is the live example (data/lab/dal_check.json): fuel came in at $3.61 a gallon against $3.15 assumed in July (+$0.46), adjusted unit revenue was up 15% year over year, and adjusted earnings per share were $1.72 against a guided $2.00 to $2.50.

Small sample: the primary curve rests on 20 quarters (2015Q1 to 2019Q4) and 7 coefficients. The ranges use the larger of the classical and Newey-West errors and Student t, and are still more likely too narrow than too wide: they assume the specification is right. The quarter-by-quarter shape is not smooth (3%, 80%, 47%, 35%, 75% for quarters 0 to 4): the fuel changes at neighbouring lags are highly correlated, so single quarters trade off against each other. The draws carry that trade-off; the share after a year is the best-determined number and the path to it is not.

One fuel cycle: the fit split is dominated by the 2014-2016 fall in fuel. Year-over-year fuel cost changes in it run from -1.89 to 0.91 cents per ASM; the latest quarter's change, +2.56, is outside that range. The curve assumes a linear response that is the same for increases and decreases and for any size of shock; the monthly industry test of asymmetry is the only check on that.

Hedging: United hedged fuel in the early 2010s and later stopped. Fuel cost here is the reported average price per gallon times gallons, and in the early sample that price includes hedge gains and losses where the release does not separate them, so the early 'shock' is partly a hedging result, not the market price.
The capacity control removes any recovery that works through capacity cuts made because of fuel. Management's own account ties recovery to capacity. The no-control variant shows the difference.
United does not define 'recover'. Our share uses a fitted baseline (constant plus capacity effect, 2013-2019); United's baseline is undisclosed. Comparing the two compares definitions.

Figures are as first printed in each quarter's earnings release. Year-over-year changes can straddle restatements and accounting changes; the 2018 change moved ancillary fees into passenger revenue, which is why the PRASM variant carries a 2018 indicator. TRASM is little affected.
The lag polynomial stops at four quarters; anything recovered later is not measured and the share is held at its four-quarter value.
Management's promise is stated for calendar quarters of one shock. Mapping it onto 'quarters after a shock' takes 2026Q2 as the first full quarter on the daily fuel series and is an assumption.

Not stable across periods. Re-estimated on all 30 quarters through 2026Q2 with no pandemic level behind them (test years included; not used for the curve), the same-quarter share is 53% (12% to 95%) against 3% on the fit split, and the one-year share 83% (53% to 113%) against 75%. A curve fitted on 2015-2019 may understate how fast United now reprices.

This two-parameter form was chosen AFTER the locked test years had been seen, because the pre-specified five-lag curve was not monotone and lost the test. Its test-split score is therefore descriptive, not a clean test. The clean test of it is the dated forward forecast for the next quarter.
The smooth curve rises steadily by construction. It cannot show an overshoot or a give-back, and it is cut at quarter 4, where the share is L x (1 - rho^5), below L when adjustment is slow.

L and rho are poorly separated: a high long-run share reached slowly fits about as well as a lower one reached fast. In the bootstrap for the published curve their correlation is 0.69, 30% of resamples sit at the upper bound of rho, and the range of L is 5.1 times as wide as the range of the one-year share. The well-determined number is the share after a year: 75% (90% range 49% to 91%). Read L and the half-life together, not one at a time.

The speed of the published curve rests on one quarter. Fitted through 2026Q1 the half-life is 2.8 quarters (rho 0.78, L 91%); adding 2026Q2 alone makes it 1.0 (rho 0.50, L 77%). Bootstrap resamples that leave that quarter out give slow curves, so the middle of the draws (18% in the shock quarter, 62% after a year) is slower than the least-squares curve (39% and 75%). The simulator samples the draws.

oos_test.definition: Predicted year-over-year change in TRASM (cents) under each response rule, given the fuel cost per ASM and capacity that actually occurred; this tests the response, not a fuel forecast. h4: four quarters ahead of the year-ago level (baseline plus the rule's fuel term). h1: one quarter ahead of the last reported quarter (last quarter's actual year-over-year change plus the change in baseline and fuel term). Each rule gets its own constant and capacity coefficient, estimated on the fit split with the fuel response held at the rule, so the rules differ only in the fuel response. A test quarter with a 2020Q1-2021Q4 level anywhere behind its prediction is left out and listed.

curve_unrestricted_draws_method.method: Joint draws of the five lag coefficients from a multivariate Student t centred on the estimates, with the cautious covariance and the regression's residual degrees of freedom; each row of curve_draws is the running sum of one coefficient draw. Not clipped and not smoothed: a draw may be negative, above 1 or non-monotone.
curve_unrestricted_draws_method.why: Covariance route rather than a block bootstrap: with 20 quarters and 7 coefficients a block bootstrap resamples only 5 blocks of four quarters and leans on a handful of them; the covariance route uses every quarter once and keeps the correlation between quarters. Student t rather than normal because the covariance is itself estimated from few quarters. Standard errors come from a cautious covariance: the classical one plus the positive part of (Newey-West minus classical), which is at least as large as both for every coefficient and every sum of coefficients. Newey-West errors are biased downward in short samples and can fall below the classical ones; this never reports the smaller. Intervals use Student t with the residual degrees of freedom. The block bootstrap is reported beside it as a check.

block_bootstrap_check.method: moving-block bootstrap of the estimation rows, block length 4

curve_unrestricted_note: The pre-specified curve: five free lag coefficients on the fit split. It was fixed before the test years were scored and it lost that test; its scores in oos_test are unchanged. It is kept for the record and is no longer what the simulator reads.

Bootstrap resamples that leave that quarter out give slow curves, so the middle of the draws (18% in the shock quarter, 62% after a year) is slower than the least-squares curve (39% and 75%). smooth.expanding_note: One entry per quarter: the curve fitted on quarters dated before as_of_period with no pandemic level behind them (all published by the time guidance for as_of_period is given). curve_p50 is the least-squares curve; no draws are stored per entry. Use these for any replay of a past quarter.
smooth.method: Partial adjustment: recovery(k) = L x (1 - rho^(k+1)) for k = 0..4 quarters after the shock. L is the share recovered in the long run and rho the part of the remaining gap left open each quarter; the half-life, ln(0.5)/ln(rho), counts quarters from the start of the shock quarter until half of L is in. Same data and definition as the five-lag regression: year-over-year change in TRASM on a constant, year-over-year capacity growth and L times the weighted sum of the year-over-year fuel cost changes at lags 0 to 4 with weights (1 - rho) rho^j. Least squares: rho on a grid from 0 to 0.95 in steps of 0.01, L in closed form given rho. Uncertainty: a moving-block bootstrap over quarters (blocks of four consecutive estimation rows, each row carrying its own lags), L and rho re-estimated on every resample; ranges are percentiles of the resamples and the draws are the resampled curves. Where the estimation rows are not contiguous (2019Q4 is followed by 2024Q1) a block can straddle the gap. The curve stops at quarter 4, where the share is L x (1 - rho^5).
smooth.post_hoc_note: This two-parameter form was chosen AFTER the locked test years had been seen, because the pre-specified five-lag curve was not monotone and lost the test. Its test-split score is therefore descriptive, not a clean test. The clean test of it is the dated forward forecast for the next quarter.
